contexts: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015). This context sheds light on why one in four incoming freshman college students leave within one year of arriving on campus [8], with a similar proportion diagnosed or treated for depression and anxiety annually [9]. These disturbing trends existed before 2020 but were exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. A meta-analysis found that 31% of college students worldwide reported symptoms of anxiety and 34% reported symptoms of depression during the early stages of the pandemic [10]. Rates varied between countries (partly due to methodo- logical differences), but American college students reported the highest rates of both anxiety (52%) and depression (69%). At one university in the United States, 18% of students had sui- cidal thoughts [11]. In studies that disaggregated data by gender, males were somewhat more likely than females to report symptoms of anxiety (36% compared to 30%), while females were much more likely than males to report symptoms of depression (56% compared to 34%). More recent research provides strong evidence for higher rates of both anxiety and depression among female college students compared to males [12–14]. A substantial body of research, dating back more than a century to Durkheim’s ground- breaking work on factors contributing to suicide, has shown that mental health challenges are mitigated by social support [15–17]. Among college students, high levels of social support are associated with reduced levels of depression and anxiety [18, 19], lower suicide risk [17], and enhanced life satisfaction and subjective well-being [20, 21]. Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified. Findings from the National College Health Assessment Loneliness continues to be an important focus for higher education leaders and practitioners, and monitoring loneliness rates provides important context. The National College Health Assessment provides multi-institutional data on college student loneliness. The American College Health Association (ACHA) conducts the NCHA annually and uses the UCLA 3-item loneliness scale to assess student loneliness (Hughes et al., 2004). The scale is comprised of three questions with the responses “hardly ever”, “some of the time” and “often”. These three options are worth 1, 2 and 3 points, respectively. The scores for each question are added together to create a total score from 3 to 9. Those with a score of six or greater are categorized as “lonely.” Loneliness in the National NCHA Sample Recent data from the national sample of university students taking the National College Health Assessment (NCHA) shows that the percentage of students reporting loneliness nationally has significantly decreased between 2022 and 2024. Table 1 shows differences in loneliness over time in the national NCHA sample between 2022 and 2024 (ACHA, 2022; ACHA, 2024).
